cases.quote: Our study had several limitations. First, the single-center design and relatively small sample size may have limited the generalizability and the statistical precision of the effect estimates. Second, the study was not powered to detect small incremental treatment effects or uncommon procedure-related adverse events. Third, the study was not designed to assess non-inferiority between the two techniques. Fourth, the reliance on the NRS pain score as the primary outcome measure may have limited the assessment of pain. Fifth, validated quality of recovery scales, such as the QoR-15 questionnaire, were not implemented. Sixth, the investigation of single-injection ESPB may not fully capture the potential analgesic benefits of continuous ESPB, which could offer prolonged pain relief [30]. In addition, variation in ESPB-related factors, including drug selection, injection volume, and technique, could have influenced the study outcomes [31,32]. Seventh, the lack of a significant difference in postoperative pain scores between the two groups may be explained by overlapping sensory coverage provided by the two block techniques. Eighth, the lack of a significant difference may also be attributable to the variable efficacy of ESPB [26,27]. Ninth, postoperative sensory dermatome mapping was not performed; therefore, although technical block performance was assessed by visualization of injectate spread, clinical extent of sensory block could not be confirmed. Tenth, some exclusion criteria specified in the IRB-approved protocol were not included in the public trial registry. Eleventh, the prospective sample-size calculation was based on a previous study reporting a mean maximum NRS pain score of 6.16 ± 1.95 within the first 24 postoperative hours in patients undergoing VATS with intercostal nerve block [14]. Twelfth, the registered primary endpoint was the 1-hour postoperative pain score, whereas the prospective sample-size calculation was based on the maximum NRS score within the first 24 postoperative hours. Thirteenth, the prespecified 12-hour NRS assessment was not collected, representing a deviation from the registered outcome-assessment schedule. This time point frequently fell around midnight or in the early hours after midnight, making standardized assessment difficult without disrupting patients’ sleep.
